title: Gita path in the world: Gandhi, Thoreau, Tilak, Vivekananda
hook: a book spoken in a chariot ended up in a jail cell in Mandalay and a cabin by Walden Pond

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Gita in your week. One verse a day, read in the morning, carried all day. Your line was carry. Did today's verse show up? Today, some people who carried it very far. Day two hundred thirty.

A young law student from Gujarat is studying in London in the late eighteen-eighties. Two brothers he has met there ask him to read the Gita with them. Embarrassed, he admits he's never read it, not even in Sanskrit or Gujarati. So he first meets it in an English poem, Edwin Arnold's The Song Celestial. His name is Mohandas Gandhi. Back in India, in Pune, a newspaper editor will one day make the Gita his life's argument. And some forty years before that, in a cabin by a pond in Massachusetts, an American was reading it in the mornings.
screen: `A LAW STUDENT IN LONDON.` → `AN ENGLISH POEM.` → `A CABIN BY A POND.`

segments.voice: Start at the pond. The first English translation of the Gita, by Charles Wilkins, appeared in 1785, and it reached New England. Henry David Thoreau took it to Walden. In Walden he wrote: "In the morning I bathe my intellect in the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Bhagvat Geeta." His friend Emerson loved it too. Then Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a leader of India's independence movement. Jailed by the British in Mandalay, in Burma, he wrote a long Marathi commentary, the Gita Rahasya, the secret of the Gita, published in 1915. His argument: the Gita's heart is karma yoga, energetic action in the world, not withdrawal from it. Swami Vivekananda, who spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, read the Gita as a call to strength. He loved Krishna's first sharp words to Arjuna in chapter two: don't give in to weakness; stand up. And Gandhi. He came to call the Gita his mother. In 1929 he finished a Gujarati translation he titled Anasakti Yoga, the yoga of non-attachment. He read the battle as the war inside every person, and drew from it selfless action and nonviolence. Tilak and Gandhi read the same book and disagreed, sharply, about whether it could justify force. That argument is still alive. Others read the Gita critically, like B. R. Ambedkar, whom we met a few days ago. All of them took it seriously enough to wrestle with it. The Gita left the chariot a long time ago. It's been in jail cells, cabins, ashrams and lecture halls. That's the word today: Gita path in the world.
screen: `THOREAU: BATHING HIS INTELLECT.` · `TILAK: ACTION, FROM A JAIL CELL.` · `VIVEKANANDA: STAND UP.` · `GANDHI: THE GITA AS MOTHER.` · then, large: `GITA PATH IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture them one by one, each reading the same book. Thoreau at dawn by the pond. Tilak in a cell, writing. Vivekananda on a stage in Chicago. Gandhi at his spinning wheel. Then picture yourself among them, with your one verse for today. You don't need to be famous to carry it. Just be the next person who does. The bell holds the time.
Gita path in the world. Thoreau at Walden, Tilak in Mandalay, Vivekananda on the road, Gandhi at home: the same book, carried and argued over, far from the chariot.
screen: `GITA PATH IN THE WORLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: who else carried it. Today, ask one older person in your life whether a verse or a saying carried them through something. Listen to the answer. Day two hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga, Tilak's Gita Rahasya and Vivekananda's talks are still widely read in India, and many Hindus know the Gita partly through these modern readings as well as the classical commentaries.

options: give up on the independence movement.
write a long commentary arguing the Gita teaches energetic action.
fork.reveal: he wrote the Gita Rahasya in Marathi, published in 1915, arguing that karma yoga is the Gita's heart.

original.note: Sanskrit: anasakti, non-attachment; Gandhi's title for his Gujarati Gita, Anasakti Yoga.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gita is an ancient book only read in temples.
what it means: it's been carried into jail cells, cabins and movements, and argued over by people who changed history.

what a scholar hears: Wilkins's 1785 translation reached the American Transcendentalists; Tilak's Gita Rahasya (1915) and Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga (1929–30) offered rival readings of action and nonviolence.

notes: Thoreau quotation is from Walden (1854), public domain, and appears in the teach in quotation marks; confirm wording against the first edition.
Gandhi's London reading with two Theosophist friends and Arnold's The Song Celestial: from his Autobiography; confirm year (c. 1888–1889).
Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga: completed 1929, published 1930; confirm.
Tilak's Mandalay imprisonment (1908–1914) and Gita Rahasya publication (1915): confirm.
Vivekananda's emphasis on Gita 2.3 is well attested in his lectures; paraphrased, not quoted.
Oppenheimer and other Western readers are left out deliberately.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Gandhi met the Gita through two Theosophist brothers after some time in London, not on arrival (hook fixed); Thoreau's Walden says 'in the morning', not 'before breakfast'; Vivekananda no longer said to have 'brought Vedanta to America' (he spoke at the 1893 Parliament in Chicago); Tilak no longer called 'young' in 1888.
